title: Mount Washington grows from "The Crossroads"

bodyMarkdown:
Northeast Bullitt County’s main town started as a junction, not a fort. Settlers called it “The Crossroads” because the Bardstown–Louisville road crossed the Shepherdsville–Shelbyville road there, near McCullough’s Run in the Salt River country. Stage traffic between Louisville and Bardstown, and between Shepherdsville and Shelbyville, made the spot a natural stop for taverns, blacksmiths, and stores long before anyone laid out lots. The surrounding land had been part of a Revolutionary War grant to David Leitch; scattered farms stood there by the 1780s.

In 1818 Catherine Drake, widow of local landowner Joseph Hough, received court permission to sell fifty acres at the crossroads to support her family. The land was divided into about eighty lots. By late 1819 most had sold, and the settlement was platted as Mount Vernon in honor of George Washington’s estate. Trustees were appointed in 1822. A naming conflict with an existing Mount Vernon in Rockcastle County forced a change. When the town incorporated in 1833, it took the name Mount Washington to keep the presidential tribute and clear the post office. A post office under the new name had already opened in 1830.

By 1847 about 700 people lived there. The town supported three churches, two schools, six stores, five doctors, two taverns, and a dozen mechanical trades. Hotels, a tannery, distilleries, a flour and lumber mill, and three limestone quarries served travelers and farmers. For a time Mount Washington was the economic heart of Bullitt County, a service center between Louisville and the Bardstown country.

The Civil War brought a brief, sharp interruption. In the autumn of 1862, during Braxton Bragg’s Kentucky Campaign, Confederate cavalry—including elements of Col. John Wharton’s brigade—held the village. On October 1–2, Union forces advancing from Louisville under Don Carlos Buell skirmished with Confederate pickets on the Bardstown Pike near Mount Washington. The Confederates burned a bridge to cover their retreat and fell back toward the Salt River. The town itself saw no major battle, but the road it sat on carried both armies toward Perryville a week later.

After the war the railroad bypassed Mount Washington, and the late nineteenth century brought stagnation. A fire on November 18, 1940, destroyed much of the downtown, including Maccabee Hall, and spurred the creation of a local fire department. Post–World War II suburban growth from Louisville, helped by industrial jobs in the metro area, reversed the decline. The old crossroads roads are now U.S. 31E and Kentucky 44; the town remains a Bullitt County hub about twenty miles southeast of Louisville.

## Kentucky today

Mount Washington is still organized around the historic crossroads. The Zack Stansbury House on Old Bardstown Road southeast of town and the Lloyd House Museum at U.S. 31E and East Street are listed on the National Register. The roads that made “The Crossroads” still carry traffic between Louisville, Bardstown, Shepherdsville, and Shelbyville.
Source: [Grokipedia: Mount Washington, Kentucky](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mount_Washington,_Kentucky)
